definition: Domesticate means to bring a wild species under human control over many generations.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word domesticate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know domesticate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Cats may have half domesticated themselves, biologists argue, drifting toward the first grain stores after the mice and staying for the saucers.
You can befriend a wild crow with peanuts — it trusts you and no one else, and nothing about the crow changes — which leaves befriending at the far, shallow end of the scale from domesticate.

Taming goes further than befriending — one animal learns to accept handling within its own lifetime, though its offspring are born as wild as ever; to domesticate claims the most, a whole species reshaped over generations until calmness is inherited rather than learned.

To breed is to choose which animals or plants leave offspring — the tool, applied one generation at a time. To domesticate is what ages of that choosing add up to: a wild species remade until tameness itself is inherited. Breeding is the means; the finished, species-deep change is domestication.

To cultivate is to grow and tend a plant on purpose — any gardener cultivates tomatoes, wild varieties included. To domesticate goes far deeper than a season's tending: generations of selection until the species itself changes, like wheat that can no longer scatter its own seed.

Domesticate means to bring a wild species under human control over many generations.
The silk moth is the extreme case in every textbook.

Fifty centuries of people choosing which caterpillars to keep have domesticated it so completely that the adult moth cannot fly, barely eats, and would not last a week outside its tray of mulberry leaves.
There is no wild silk moth to return it to; the species itself has been reshaped, era by era, into a creature whose whole world is human hands.
Domesticate is the exact word because it means to bring a wild species under human control over many generations — the plural matters.
No one moth was ever won over; breeders selected parents for age upon age until tameness was born in, not taught.
That species-deep change is what separates domestication from anything one patient keeper can do.
Domesticate is a species-scale word: biologists use it for the long, inherited change that turned wolves toward dogs and wild grasses toward wheat.
For one animal won over in one lifetime, the honest word is tame — a raccoon can be tamed by autumn, but no keeper alive will domesticate one.
Used of people or rivers, it is a picture borrowed from the barnyard, and it keeps the same core: brought under control, made at home.

Nine thousand years ago, a Mexican grass called teosinte carried a dozen hard little kernels locked in a stony case.
Farmers who saved seed from the loosest, largest ears slowly turned that grass into maize, the corn that now feeds much of the world.
The change runs so deep that scientists say those farmers did not merely improve the plant — they domesticated it entirely.
A modern ear of corn cannot even reproduce by itself: its kernels sit clamped to the cob, waiting for a hand to plant them.
Drop a whole ear on the ground and the seedlings come up in a strangling clump; the species now depends on us as surely as we once depended on it.
